claim: Sugars that contain glucose, such as sucrose, are generally preferred to artificial sweeteners owing to their post-ingestive rewarding effect, which elevates striatal dopamine (DA) release.
source: Sugars that contain glucose, such as sucrose, are generally preferred to artificial sweeteners owing to their post-ingestive rewarding effect, which elevates striatal dopamine (DA) release.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Smiciklas-Wright et al., 2002; Jacobson, 2005; Domingos et al., 2011; Sicher, 2011) and established knowledge about dopamine's role in reward.

claim: Optogenetic activation of melanin-concentrating hormone (MCH) neurons during intake of the artificial sweetener sucralose increases striatal dopamine levels.
source: In this study, we show that optogenetic activation of melanin-concentrating hormone (MCH) neurons during intake of the artificial sweetener sucralose increases striatal dopamine levels and inverts the normal preference for sucrose vs sucralose.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3, showing microdialysis measurements of dopamine release during optogenetic stimulation.

claim: Optogenetic activation of MCH neurons during sucralose intake inverts the normal preference for sucrose vs sucralose.
source: In this study, we show that optogenetic activation of melanin-concentrating hormone (MCH) neurons during intake of the artificial sweetener sucralose increases striatal dopamine levels and inverts the normal preference for sucrose vs sucralose.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data in Figure 2 showing preference reversal with optogenetic stimulation.

claim: Animals with ablation of MCH neurons no longer prefer sucrose to sucralose.
source: Conversely, animals with ablation of MCH neurons no longer prefer sucrose to sucralose and show reduced striatal DA release upon sucrose ingestion.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral preference data in Figure 5A showing loss of sucrose preference in MCH-ablated mice.

claim: Animals with ablation of MCH neurons show reduced striatal DA release upon sucrose ingestion.
source: Conversely, animals with ablation of MCH neurons no longer prefer sucrose to sucralose and show reduced striatal DA release upon sucrose ingestion.
evidence: This claim is supported by microdialysis data in Figure 4 showing reduced dopamine release in MCH-ablated mice drinking sucrose.

claim: MCH neurons project to reward areas.
source: We further show that MCH neurons project to reward areas and are required for the post-ingestive rewarding effect of sucrose in sweet-blind Trpm5−/− mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 showing MCH projections to striatum and midbrain.

claim: MCH neurons are required for the post-ingestive rewarding effect of sucrose in sweet-blind Trpm5−/− mice.
source: We further show that MCH neurons project to reward areas and are required for the post-ingestive rewarding effect of sucrose in sweet-blind Trpm5−/− mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by conditioning data in Figure 5D showing loss of sucrose conditioning in sweet-blind MCH-ablated mice.

claim: The post-ingestive rewarding effect of sucrose was first described by showing that non-nutritive liquids that are paired to glucose administration either in the intra-gastric tract or in plasma, are greatly preferred over liquids that are not paired with nutrients.
source: This post-ingestive rewarding effect of sucrose was first described by showing that non-nutritive liquids that are paired to glucose administration either in the intra-gastric tract or in plasma, are greatly preferred over liquids that are not paired with nutrients (de Araujo et al., 2008; Ren et al., 2010; de Araujo et al., 2010; Oliveira-Maia et al., 2011; Sclafani et al., 2011; Fernstrom et al., 2012; de Araujo et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Sweet-blind Trpm5 knockout mice can still sense the nutrient value of sucrose.
source: In addition, sweet-blind Trpm5 knockout mice can still sense the nutrient value of sucrose (de Araujo et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Sucrose but not artificial sweeteners such as sucralose can drive dopamine (DA) release in the midbrain even in the absence of taste.
source: Rodent studies have further shown that sucrose but not artificial sweeteners such as sucralose can drive dopamine (DA) release in the midbrain even in the absence of taste (de Araujo et al., 2008; Ren et al., 2010; de Araujo et al., 2010; Oliveira-Maia et al., 2011; Sclafani et al., 2011; Fernstrom et al., 2012; de Araujo et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous rodent studies.

claim: The combination of sweet taste plus an increase of dopamine accounts for the preference for natural vs artificial sweeteners.
source: The combination of sweet taste plus an increase of dopamine accounts for the preference for natural vs artificial sweeteners (Domingos et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The artificial sweetener sucralose is preferred to sucrose only if supplemented by a proxy for this post-ingestive reward in the form of optogenetic activation of DA neurons.
source: We previously reported that the artificial sweetener sucralose is preferred to sucrose only if supplemented by a proxy for this post-ingestive reward in the form of optogenetic activation of DA neurons (Domingos et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: MCH neurons in the lateral hypothalamus (LH) are glucose sensitive, and show increased activity when extracellular glucose levels increase.
source: Melanin-concentrating hormone-expressing neurons (Pmch or, MCH neurons; in accordance with previous literature [Shimada et al., 1998; Alon and Friedman, 2006; Kong et al., 2010], we adopt the later nomenclature throughout this report) in the lateral hypothalamus (LH) are glucose sensitive, and show increased activity when extracellular glucose levels increase (Burdakov et al., 2005; Kong et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Pmch knockout and MCH neuronal ablation lead to reduced body weight, indicating a critical role of these neurons in the regulation of energy balance.
source: Pmch knockout and MCH neuronal ablation lead to reduced body weight, indicating a critical role of these neurons in the regulation of energy balance (Shimada et al., 1998; Whiddon and Palmiter, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MCH neurons send dense projections to reward centers in the striatum and midbrain where dopaminergic neurons are located.
source: In addition, MCH neurons send dense projections to reward centers in the striatum and midbrain where dopaminergic neurons are located (current report).
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical data presented in the current manuscript (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: 97 ± 3% of MCH neurons expressed ChR2-YFP in Pmch-ChR2 mice.
source: In addition, 97 ± 3% of MCH neurons expressed ChR2-YFP (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 92 ± 8% of ChR2-YFP neurons expressed MCH in Pmch-ChR2 mice.
source: The YFP signal was seen in the LH with the characteristic appearance of MCH neurons (Figure 1A), and there was a 92 ± 8% overlap of YFP and MCH.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings in slice preparations confirmed light-evoked spiking at 5, 10, and 20 Hz in MCH neurons expressing ChR2.
source: Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings in slice preparations confirmed light-evoked spiking at 5, 10, and 20 Hz (Figure 1C), as well as during continuous light pulses of one second (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The spike rate of MCH neurons was higher with light pulses of 20 Hz vs 5 Hz.
source: The spike rate of MCH neurons was higher with light pulses of 20 Hz vs 5 Hz.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Glucose has been shown to evoke similar high-frequency bursting of MCH neurons.
source: Note, glucose has been shown to evoke similar high-frequency bursting of MCH neurons (see inset, Figure 1D) (Burdakov et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Spike attenuation during optogenetic stimulation was similar to what has been previously reported for glucose-triggered responses in MCH neurons.
source: Spike attenuation (Figure 1D, inset) during optogenetic stimulation was similar to what has been previously reported for glucose-triggered responses (Burdakov et al., 2005; Kong et al., 2010) in MCH neurons, and changes in membrane potential were resilient to optical stimulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to cited previous studies and data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: ChR2(+) and ChR2(–) mice had equal preference for water+laser vs water alone at all stimulation frequencies tested.
source: ChR2(+) and ChR2(–) mice had equal preference for water+laser vs water alone at all stimulation frequencies tested (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In the absence of ChR2 or at a low stimulation frequency of 5 Hz, animals still preferred sucrose to sucralose.
source: In the absence of ChR2 (gray bars in Figure 2) or at a low stimulation frequency of 5 Hz (Figure 2A), animals still preferred sucrose to sucralose.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A light frequency of 20 Hz inverted an animal's preference with a strong preference for sucralose plus MCH activation relative to sucrose.
source: However, consistent with the greater effect of 20 Hz on spiking of MCH neurons in slice preparation, a light frequency of 20 Hz, as well as continuous light, inverted an animal's preference with a strong preference for sucralose plus MCH activation relative to sucrose (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: At 20 Hz, ChR2(–) mice displayed a preference ratio for sucrose of 82.2 ± 3%, whereas ChR2(+) mice had a sucrose preference ratio of 20.0 ± 4%.
source: At 20 Hz, ChR2(–) mice (Figure 2B, middle panel, gray bars) displayed a preference ratio for sucrose of 82.2 ± 3%, whereas ChR2(+) mice had a sucrose preference ratio of 20.0 ± 4% (Figure 2B, middle panel, blue bars).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Under continuous light, ChR2(–) mice displayed a preference ratio for sucrose of 76.7 ± 3%, whereas ChR2(+) mice displayed a preference ratio for sucrose of 26.8 ± 5%.
source: Under continuous light, ChR2(–) mice displayed a preference ratio for sucrose of 76.7 ± 3% (Figure 2B, right panel, gray bars), whereas ChR2(+) mice displayed a preference ratio for sucrose of 26.8 ± 5% (Figure 2B, right panel, blue bars).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: MCH neurons densely innervate the striatum and the ventral midbrain, making synapses onto DA neurons.
source: The post-ingestive rewarding effect of glucose is associated with an increase of DA release in the striatum (de Araujo et al., 2013; de Araujo et al., 2008; de Araujo et al., 2010; Ren et al., 2010), and we confirmed that MCH neurons densely innervate the striatum and the ventral midbrain, making synapses onto DA neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This claim is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Animals drinking sucralose without light stimulation displayed negligible changes in striatal DA levels.
source: As previously reported, animals drinking sucralose (without light stimulation) displayed negligible changes in striatal DA levels (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by microdialysis data shown in Figure 3B and citation to previous reports.

claim: Animals drinking sucralose when the laser was set to OFF displayed an overall 8.2 ± 2.6% change from baseline DA.
source: Animals drinking sucralose when the laser was set to OFF displayed an overall 8.2 ± 2.6% change from baseline DA (average across all S1–S5 samples); this change was not significantly different from baseline (gray bars in Figure 3E p>0.05, one sample T-test against 100% baseline).
evidence: This claim is supported by microdialysis data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: When sucralose ingestion was coupled to laser stimulation of MCH neurons, DA release significantly increased in the striatum.
source: However, when sucralose ingestion was coupled to laser stimulation of MCH neurons, DA release significantly increased in the striatum (**p<0.008; Figure 3C–G, blue bars).
evidence: This claim is supported by microdialysis data shown in Figure 3C-G.

claim: When laser was set to ON during ingestion of sucralose, DA levels increased 68.7 ± 9% vs baseline DA.
source: When laser was set to ON during ingestion of sucralose, DA levels increased 68.7 ± 9% vs baseline DA (average across all S1–S5 samples, blue bars in Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by microdialysis data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Optogenetic activation of MCH neurons markedly increased sucralose ingestion during the laser ON condition.
source: Optogenetic activation of MCH neurons markedly increased sucralose ingestion during the laser ON condition (*p<0.05; Figure 3F) while activation of MCH neurons did not change intake of water (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of MCH neurons paired to water was not preferred to water alone, showing that activation of MCH neurons is not rewarding in the absence of sucralose.
source: As mentioned above, optogenetic stimulation of MCH neurons paired to water was not preferred to water alone, showing that activation of MCH neurons is not rewarding in the absence of sucralose.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Both MCH activation and the presence of sucralose were required to establish a change of preference.
source: Thus, both MCH activation and the presence of sucralose were required to establish a change of preference.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined results showing that MCH activation alone (with water) does not change preference, but MCH activation with sucralose does.

claim: Control mice drinking sucrose displayed significantly higher dopamine levels compared to MCH-ablated mice.
source: MCH-ablated (Pmch-CRE-LSL-DTR+DT) and control mice (Pmch-CRE-LSL-DTR+veh, and LSL-DTR+DT) were subjected to microdialysis sampling of striatal DA during sucrose ingestion (Figure 4B). Control mice drinking sucrose displayed significantly higher dopamine levels compared to MCH-ablated mice (Figure 4C–F; **p<0.008 ANOVA in Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by microdialysis data shown in Figure 4C-F.

claim: Control mice showed an overall 118.3 ± 0.3% increase in striatal DA levels while drinking sucrose.
source: Control mice showed an overall 118.3 ± 0.3% increase in striatal DA levels while drinking sucrose (average across all S1–5 samples, Figure 4F, ***p<1.98e10−9 T-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by microdialysis data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: MCH-ablated mice showed a negligible DA efflux during sucrose intake, and the levels after sucrose exposure did not differ from baseline levels.
source: In contrast to animals without DT injection, MCH-ablated mice showed a negligible DA efflux during sucrose intake, and the levels after sucrose exposure did not differ from baseline levels (p>0.4, one sample T-test compared to 100% baseline).
evidence: This claim is supported by microdialysis data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Baseline DA levels were similar in both MCH-ablated and control groups.
source: Baseline DA levels were similar in both groups (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: MCH-ablated mice consumed significantly less sucrose than control mice when given free access to sucrose or water.
source: Consistent with a lower reward value of sucrose, when given free access to sucrose or water, MCH-ablated mice consumed significantly less sucrose than control mice (Figure 4G, *p<0.05 ANOVA), while water intake was equivalent between the groups (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Water intake was equivalent between MCH-ablated and control groups.
source: Consistent with a lower reward value of sucrose, when given free access to sucrose or water, MCH-ablated mice consumed significantly less sucrose than control mice (Figure 4G, *p<0.05 ANOVA), while water intake was equivalent between the groups (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Preference ratios for sucrose in Pmch-CRE;LSL-DTR(+veh), LSL-DTR(+DT) and Pmch-CRE;LSL-DTR(+DT) mice were, respectively, 77.1 ± 7%, 82.0 ± 4%, and 39.9 ± 5%.
source: Preference ratios for sucrose in Pmch-CRE;LSL-DTR(+veh), LSL-DTR(+DT) and Pmch-CRE;LSL-DTR(+DT) mice were, respectively, 77.1 ± 7%, 82.0 ± 4%, and 39.9 ± 5%.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: While control mice preferred sucrose to sucralose, MCH-ablated mice no longer had a preference for sucrose.
source: While control mice preferred sucrose to sucralose, MCH-ablated mice no longer had a preference for sucrose. This reduction in sucrose preference is statistically significant (Figure 5A, *p<0.0012, ¥p<0.009, T-test with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons, same-symbol pairs indicate statistically significant differences; see also Figure 5—figure supplement 1 for total licks in each).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: MCH neuronal ablation did not alter an animal's preference for either sucrose or sucralose vs water.
source: However, MCH neuronal ablation did not alter an animal's preference for either sucrose or sucralose vs water indicating that, in contrast to their requirement for establishing the post-ingestive effect of sucrose, MCH neurons are not required for establishing a preference for sweet taste (Figure 5B,C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: MCH neurons are not required for establishing a preference for sweet taste.
source: However, MCH neuronal ablation did not alter an animal's preference for either sucrose or sucralose vs water indicating that, in contrast to their requirement for establishing the post-ingestive effect of sucrose, MCH neurons are not required for establishing a preference for sweet taste (Figure 5B,C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that MCH-ablated mice still prefer sweet substances over water.

claim: The postprandial increase in blood glucose after sucrose ingestion was normal in MCH-ablated animals.
source: The postprandial increase in blood glucose after sucrose ingestion was normal in MCH-ablated animals (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2), demonstrating that the changes in sucrose preference were not a result of any differences in blood glucose levels (Kong et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by blood glucose data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Activation of MCH neurons are necessary and sufficient for establishing the preference of animals for sucrose compared to artificial sweeteners.
source: Altogether, these data indicate that activation of MCH neurons are necessary and sufficient for establishing the preference of animals for sucrose compared to artificial sweeteners.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined gain-of-function and loss-of-function experiments showing that MCH activation inverts preference and MCH ablation eliminates sucrose preference.

claim: Sweet-blind control mice showed a significant side bias towards the bottle where sucrose was placed during the conditioning sessions.
source: Sweet-blind control mice showed a significant side bias towards the side where sucrose was placed during the conditioning sessions, in which sucrose or sucralose are delivered at opposite sides on alternate days, (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by conditioning data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Sweet-blind MCH-ablated mice did not show a preference in the conditioning protocol, indicating that the post-ingestive rewarding effect of sucrose had been lost.
source: In contrast, sweet-blind MCH-ablated mice did not show a preference in this conditioning protocol, indicating that the post-ingestive rewarding effect of sucrose had been lost.
evidence: This claim is supported by conditioning data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Trpm5–/– Pmch-CRE;LSL-DTR+veh and Trpm5–/–LSL-DTR+DT control mice showed conditioned side preferences of 70 ± 3% and 79 ± 5% respectively, towards the side where sucrose was placed.
source: Trpm5–/– Pmch-CRE;LSL-DTR+veh and Trpm5–/–LSL-DTR+DT control mice showed conditioned side preferences of 70 ± 3% and 79 ± 5% respectively, towards the side where sucrose was placed.
evidence: This claim is supported by conditioning data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Trpm5–/– Pmch-CRE;-LSL-DTR(+DT) mice had 50 ± 7% conditioned side preference towards the side where sucrose was placed.
source: Trpm5–/– Pmch-CRE;-LSL-DTR(+DT) mice had 50 ± 7% conditioned side preference towards the side where sucrose was placed.
evidence: This claim is supported by conditioning data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The behavioral conditioning by the post-ingestive rewarding effect of sucrose in sweet-blind Trpm5–/– mice positively correlates with the extent of DA neuron activation, as assayed by staining for cFos in DA neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTA).
source: Finally, the behavioral conditioning by the post-ingestive rewarding effect of sucrose in sweet-blind Trpm5–/– mice positively correlates with the extent of DA neuron activation, as assayed by staining for cFos in DA neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by cFos staining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: MCH neurons are required for sensing the nutrient value of sucrose in the absence of taste.
source: These data confirm that MCH neurons are required for sensing the nutrient value of sucrose in the absence of taste.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the conditioning experiments in sweet-blind mice showing loss of sucrose conditioning in MCH-ablated animals.

claim: MCH neurons are necessary and sufficient for establishing a preference for sucrose vs sucralose.
source: In this manuscript, we report that MCH neurons are necessary and sufficient for establishing a preference for sucrose vs sucralose, an artificial sweetener.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined gain-of-function and loss-of-function experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: MCH neurons serve as an essential link between glucose sensing and sugar reward.
source: MCH neurons serve as an essential link between glucose sensing and sugar reward, and these data thus identify a key component of the neural circuit that establishes the preference for natural vs artificial sweeteners (Smiciklas-Wright et al., 2002; Jacobson, 2005; Domingos et al., 2011; Sicher, 2011).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined results showing MCH neurons respond to glucose and regulate reward-related dopamine release.

claim: It is possible that glucose is sensed elsewhere, such as by putative gastric/intestinal sensors or other nutrient sensors, which inform the brain and MCH neurons about the nutrient content of ingested food.
source: However, it is also possible that glucose is sensed elsewhere, such as by putative gastric/intestinal sensors or other nutrient sensors, which inform the brain and MCH neurons about the nutrient content of ingested food (Sclafani et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is speculative, discussing alternative mechanisms for glucose sensing.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of MCH neurons alone is not sufficient to alter behavior in the absence of taste.
source: We note, however, that optogenetic stimulation of MCH neurons alone is not sufficient to alter behavior in the absence of taste.
evidence: This claim is supported by the observation that MCH activation with water does not change preference (Figure 2A).

claim: MCH neurons are components of a reward-encoding network that integrates information from multiple sources, including the nutrients themselves, lingual taste buds and, possibly, other sites of glucose sensing like the gut.
source: The data thus suggest that MCH neurons are components of a reward-encoding network that integrates information from multiple sources, including the nutrients themselves, lingual taste buds and, possibly, other sites of glucose sensing like the gut.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the requirement for both sweet taste and MCH activation to drive reward.

claim: Viral tracing from lingual taste buds shows that MCH neurons are part of a circuit processing gustatory information.
source: Consistent with this possibility, viral tracing from lingual taste buds shows that MCH neurons are part of a circuit processing gustatory information (Pérez et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The role of MCH neurons contrasts with that of DA neurons, which upon optogenetic stimulation have been shown to be rewarding when paired to water.
source: The role of MCH neurons uncovered here contrasts with that of DA neurons, which upon optogenetic stimulation have been shown to be rewarding when paired to water (Domingos et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study and comparison to current results.

claim: A synergy between taste and the post-ingestive rewarding effect would explain why sucrose and other fructose/glucose disaccharides, which are more potent stimulators of sweet-taste receptors than glucose alone, are generally preferred to glucose alone.
source: A synergy between taste and the post-ingestive rewarding effect would explain why sucrose and other fructose/glucose disaccharides, which are more potent stimulators of sweet-taste receptors than glucose alone, are generally preferred to glucose alone (Sclafani and Mann, 1987; Nelson et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing an explanation for observed preferences based on synergy between taste and post-ingestive effects.

claim: The activity of MCH neurons is increased by glucose.
source: As mentioned, the activity of MCH neurons is increased by glucose (Burdakov et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Glucose-activated MCH neurons and pancreatic β cells share signal transduction components necessary for glucose sensing.
source: Glucose-activated MCH neurons and pancreatic β cells share signal transduction components necessary for glucose sensing, and both Kir6.2 and UCP2 regulate glucose excitability of MCH neurons (Kong et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: A loss of function of Kir6.1 in MCH neurons leads to alterations in results of a glucose tolerance test with increased plasma glucose at later times.
source: Moreover, a loss of function of Kir6.1 in MCH neurons leads to alterations in results of a glucose tolerance test with increased plasma glucose at later times, establishing a role for these neurons in glucose homeostasis (Kong et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Orexin/hypocretin-containing neurons can also sense glucose.
source: For example, orexin/hypocretin-containing neurons can also sense glucose and it is thus possible that these or other neural populations in the mesolimbic system, or higher order centers can also influence the reward value of sugar (Burdakov et al., 2005; Karnani and Burdakov, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Both MCH knockout and MCH ablated mice show augmented locomotor responses to psychostimulant drugs.
source: Previous reports have also explored the relationship between MCH neurons and reward: both MCH knockout and MCH ablated mice show augmented locomotor responses to psychostimulant drugs (Pissios et al., 2008; Whiddon and Palmiter, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Loss of function of MCHR-1 recreates the locomotor phenotypes seen in Pmch−/− mice: Mchr1−/− mice are super-sensitive to the locomotor activating effects of d-amphetamine.
source: Loss of function of MCHR-1 recreates the locomotor phenotypes seen in Pmch−/− mice: Mchr1−/− mice are super-sensitive to the locomotor activating effects of d-amphetamine (Smith et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The levels of cFos in dopaminergic neurons of the VTA are reduced in MCH-ablated, sweet-blind Trpm5 KO mice given sucrose.
source: Consistent with this, the levels of cFos in dopaminergic neurons of the VTA are reduced in MCH-ablated, sweet-blind Trpm5 KO mice given sucrose.
evidence: This claim is supported by cFos staining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: MCH neurons do not appear to express the leptin receptor.
source: The effects of leptin on reward are unlikely to be a result of a direct effect on MCH neurons as they do not appear to express the leptin receptor (Leinninger et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: A distinct neural population in the LH expressing neurotensin respond to leptin.
source: However, a distinct neural population in the LH expressing neurotensin respond to leptin, and further studies may reveal whether or not leptin reduces MCH activity indirectly by activating these cells (Leinninger et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Ablation of MCH neurons attenuates the obese phenotype of leptin deficient ob/ob mice indicating that MCH neurons are downstream of leptin action.
source: Ablation of MCH neurons attenuates the obese phenotype of leptin deficient ob/ob mice indicating that MCH neurons are downstream of leptin action (Alon and Friedman, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: It is possible that the reduced food intake in MCH-ablated animals is a result of a loss of the reward value of nutrient in these animals.
source: Ablation of MCH neurons causes hypophagia and leanness, and it is possible that the reduced food intake is a result of a loss of the reward value of nutrient in these animals (Alon and Friedman, 2006).
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a mechanism for the hypophagia observed in MCH-ablated mice.

claim: Leptin has been recently reported to have a presynaptic action to suppress excitatory synaptic input onto VTA DA neurons.
source: The reward value of sugar is also regulated by leptin, which has been recently reported to have a presynaptic action to suppress excitatory synaptic input onto VTA DA neurons (Domingos et al., 2011; Thompson and Borgland, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The market share of sugared soda is nearly triple that of diet soda.
source: The market share of sugared soda is nearly triple that of diet soda (Smiciklas-Wright et al., 2002; Jacobson, 2005; Sicher, 2011), and our data suggest a biological approach to potentially regulate sugar consumption.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous reports on market data.

claim: Blocking dopamine transmission with haloperidol suppressed preference for sucrose versus sucralose.
source: (A) Blocking dopamine transmission with haloperidol (hal) suppressed preference for sucrose versus sucralose. In 10 min, wild-type animals injected with hal (ip, 1 mg/kg) showed a preference ratio for sucrose of 51 ± 7%, whereas vehicle treated animals showed a preference ratio for sucrose of 79 ± 4%.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Intracranial injection of 1 ng/g of diphtheria toxin led to a complete loss of MCH neurons in Pmch-CRE;LSL-DTR mice.
source: We injected Pmch-CRE;LSL-DTR mice with diphtheria toxin (+DT) or vehicle (+veh) intracranially (1 ng/g of body weight). This dose led to a complete loss of MCH neurons (Figure 4A, see Figure 4—figure supplement 1 for other doses).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: At a dose of 1 ng per gram of animal, 0.3 ± 0.18 neuron/section marked with MCH could be visualized under fluorescence microscopy, which is not significantly different from zero.
source: At a dose of 1 ng per gram of animal, 0.3 ± 0.18 neuron/section marked with MCH could be visualized under fluorescence microscopy. Statistically, this amount is not significantly different from zero (p>0.05, One sample t test against zero).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Baseline DA concentration of ablated MCH-Cre; LSL-DTR+DT mice (0.34 ± 0.09pg/μl) were not significantly different from control MCH-Cre; LSL-DTR+veh mice (0.25 ± 0.05pg/μl).
source: (A) Baseline DA concentration of ablated MCH-Cre; LSL-DTR+DT mice (0.34 ± 0.09pg/μl) were not significantly different from control MCH-Cre; LSLDTR+veh mice (0.25 ± 0.05pg/μl)(p>0.22, t test), thus excluding chronic effects of MCH neuronal ablation on DA levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by baseline dopamine measurement data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.
